article_content: Table Mountain, Cape Town (CNN) -- For hundreds of millions of years, it has dominated the southern African coastal skyline, providing a dramatic backdrop to an idyllic location. Table Mountain, recently voted one of the 'New Seven Wonders of Nature' by a global audience, now joins the ranks of the Amazon rainforest and other exotic sites throughout Asia. My task for 'Inside Africa' is to meet the people living in its shadow, connected to its spirit. The first people to live near this majestic mountain were the Khoi, who migrated here around 2,000 years ago. As I hike through its rugged terrain near Lion's Head, I meet Kerneels, a direct descendant of the Khoi. He shows me a sacred place he visits regularly. 'This is wild sage,' he says, handing me some. 'We burn it to release negative energy.' We trek for 30 minutes, off the hiking trail, up the steep terrain. Kerneels explains that every plant around us was used by his ancestors. When we arrive at the shrine, I see large rocks grouped together overlooking the coastline and South Atlantic Ocean. It's beautiful and peaceful. Kerneels shares the challenges of being one of the few remaining Khoi people. Their philosophy was to use only what you need and respect all forms of life on the mountain. I meet Caron von Zeil, founder of the 'Reclaim Camissa' project, at the foot of Table Mountain. She's working to restore the natural waterways that were closed off as the city grew. Caron explains that her research shows there's enough fresh water in the system for local residents. Despite facing challenges, she remains committed to the project.

article_content: Recently, a significant security breach occurred when Russian hackers compromised LinkedIn, releasing millions of passwords online. Shortly after, dating site eHarmony reported a similar attack, with speculation that the same hackers were responsible due to the similar nature of the breaches and their close timing. Experts like Graham Cluley from Sophos Security advise that users should focus on creating 'long, hard-to-crack, unique passwords' that aren't dictionary words or simple sequences. To check if your password was among those stolen, LastPass has provided a tool for both LinkedIn and eHarmony users. It's also crucial to use different passwords across different sites. Tools like KeePass, 1password, and LastPass can securely store multiple passwords.

post_content: 'Stay safe online! Recent hacks on LinkedIn and eHarmony show the importance of using strong, unique passwords. Check if you've been affected and switch to password managers like LastPass! #OnlineSecurity #PasswordProtection'

article_content: A devastating multi-car crash on Florida's Interstate 75 in Gainesville resulted in 11 fatalities and 46 injuries due to a combination of heavy fog and smoke from a nearby brush fire. The Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) investigated the incident and concluded that drivers were responsible for the crash by failing to slow down despite 'Fog/Smoke' warning signs. The FHP report stated that patrol officers acted reasonably in reopening the interstate after monitoring the conditions. The decision to reopen was made after on-site incident commanders determined the roadway was clear, despite warnings from some officers that conditions could deteriorate quickly.

article_content: The cost of attending college in the 'United States' is becoming increasingly expensive, with some institutions charging over '$60,000' per year for tuition alone. According to the 'Department of Education', 'New York University' tops the list as the most expensive college, with an annual tuition fee of '$61,977'. When considering the total cost of attendance, including room, board, and fees, the price for a 'four-year degree' at top colleges can exceed '$240,000'. The rising costs of higher education have led to growing 'student loan debt', an issue exacerbated by the recent doubling of 'interest rates' on 'student loans'.

article_content: A University of Melbourne study found that children of same-sex couples have better general health and family cohesion than those from traditional families. The study surveyed 315 same-sex parents and their 500 children, showing a 6% higher score in general health and family cohesion. Dr Simon Crouch, the lead researcher, stated that the equitable sharing of responsibilities in same-sex households contributes to a more harmonious environment. However, the study also highlighted that about two-thirds of these children experience stigma related to their parents' sexual orientation.

article_content: Vets have performed one of the world's smallest amputations on a field mouse run over by a wheelie bin. The rodent, named Mickey, was injured when Debra Tuck, 51, put out her rubbish in Seaham, County Durham. Despite a slim chance of survival, vets at Westway Veterinary Group carried out surgery to remove his crushed leg. Mrs Tuck has decided to keep Mickey as a pet despite admitting she's 'petrified' of mice. The operation, authorised by Westway director Jason Atherton, was successful, and Mickey has made a remarkable recovery.

article_content: The families of dozens of dead children whose identities were used in undercover police operations will likely never know if their children's names were among those used, police revealed yesterday. The practice, known as the 'Day of the Jackal' deception, was described as 'morally repugnant' by Chief Constable Mick Creedon, who led the review into the scandal. The review found that at least 42 children's identities were used by Scotland Yard.

article_content: A 27-year-old man from 'Los Angeles', 'Leroy Barnes', has been accused of committing 'disability fraud' by collecting over '$51,000' in workers' compensation benefits between '2010' and '2011'. article_content: NEW YORK -- Federal agents raided the home of Brianna Suggs, a top fundraiser and longtime confidante to New York City Mayor Eric Adams, on Thursday. Adams abruptly canceled a planned White House meeting and flew back to New York. The FBI confirmed a 'court-authorized law enforcement action' at Suggs' Brooklyn home. Suggs is a campaign consultant who raised money for Adams' election and lobbied his administration for a real estate client. The raid happened shortly after Adams canceled several Washington, D.C. meetings, including one with senior White House officials. Adams' campaign said it 'has always held itself to the highest standards' and will comply with any inquiries.

article_content: LONDON, England (CNN) -- Asia, covering over one-third of the world's surface and home to around four billion people across 70 countries, significantly contributes to global film production. It produces half of the world's films, with Bollywood alone producing around 1,000 films each year, almost twice as many as Hollywood. The continent has given rise to many influential directors, actors, and film genres. For instance, Ang Lee's 'Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon' (2000) pays homage to the Chinese fantasy martial arts genre, Wuxia. Japan's unique horror genre is exemplified in Takashi Shimizu's 'Ju-on: The Grudge.' Other notable films include Wong Kar-Wai's 'In the Mood for Love,' Mehboob Khan's 'Mother India,' Bong Joon-ho's 'The Host,' and Akira Kurosawa's 'Ikiru.'

article_content: A new wearable device called 'LeapBand' has been released, targeting children aged four to seven. It's designed to track activity, download apps, and play games, helping parents monitor their child's exercise levels. The $40 device features motion sensors, a high-resolution color screen, and a rechargeable battery. It comes preloaded with 50 activities and challenges that track a child's physical movements, rewarding them with points for their virtual pet. Activities include 'Walk like a crab' and 'Spin like a helicopter'. LeapFrog claims that 'LeapBand' encourages active play and healthy habits. The device is available in various colors and comes with customizable pets from the 'Pet Pals' franchise.

article_content: Residents of Cape Coral, Florida, have reported seeing unidentified flying objects (UFOs) in the night sky. article_content: A 'Sudan' court has upheld the death sentence for four 'radical Islamists' convicted of killing an 'American intelligence officer' and his 'Sudanese escort' in 'January 2008'. The diplomat's mother in the 'United States' requested the court to uphold the previous ruling. Four 'Islamists' were sentenced to death by hanging for killing 'American spy' John Granville. Judge Sayed Ahmed Al-Badry cited 'Islamic texts' that condemn killing 'Muslims and non-Muslims'. He emphasized that taking another person's life is a 'grave sin'. The defendants called Granville an 'infidel' and argued that 'Muslims should not be executed for killing non-believers'. Granville, working for the 'U.S. Agency for International Development', was killed along with his 'Sudanese bodyguard', Abdel Rahman Abbas. The men were shot after a 'New Year's Eve Party' in 2008. The death sentence was originally passed in 'June'. Under 'Sudan's Islamic law', the victim's family can request the death penalty, forgive, or seek 'blood money'. Some of Abbas' family members had pardoned the killers, according to 'media reports'. However, Granville's mother requested the execution in a letter read out in court. Granville's lawyer, Taha Ibrahim, deemed the court's ruling 'just'. 'The court passed the death sentence by hanging as per her wish,' Ibrahim said. 'It's the legal sentence, proper and according to the law, and it will be executed.' The four men claimed innocence, stating they were convicted in a 'kangaroo court' with 'videotaped confessions' extracted under 'duress'. They have 15 days to appeal.

article_content: U.S. President Barack Obama says the fight against 'out-of-control' Ebola remains 'extremely challenging', with cases 'skyrocketing' in Sierra Leone and a doctor contracting the disease there before dying in the U.S. on Monday. The president spoke at the White House Tuesday after a briefing with his Ebola response team, stressing that the continued outbreak in West Africa makes a 'long-term and aggressive' fight against the disease 'absolutely vital'. 'It underscores the importance of pushing forward until we completely eradicate this disease in that region,' Obama said, noting the situation is 'more dire than ever'. Obama expressed 'deep sorrow' over Dr. Martin Salia's death, a Sierra Leone citizen and U.S. legal resident who arrived for treatment at the Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha on Saturday. He became the second person in the U.S. to die from Ebola, following Thomas Eric Duncan, who died at a Texas hospital after contracting the disease in Liberia. Obama noted that treatment in the U.S. generally has a 'much better' outcome, stating that prompt diagnosis and treatment offer a 'great chance of curing' Ebola, as seen in the recovery of all eight patients treated promptly in the U.S. However, until the outbreak ends in West Africa, Obama warned of a 'significant risk' to people worldwide, citing the World Health Organization's report of a 'steep increase' in the Ebola death toll. U.S. Congress members are examining ways to help West Africa cope with the outbreak, with some calling for a 'massive overhaul' of current response efforts. article_content: Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov asserts that the West misinterprets President Vladimir Putin's remarks as 'anti-U.S. rhetoric' or an attempt to 'spark another Cold War,' with sources close to the Kremlin hinting at a more aggressive intent. In Sunday's Washington Post, Lavrov noted that Mr. Putin's words were just a 'routine statement' and that he had already raised these 'minor concerns' with the Bush administration. At a recent Munich speech, Mr. Putin allegedly stated that the U.S. is 'secretly fueling' a new global arms race by using 'undeclared force' and making other countries feel 'extremely insecure.' Lavrov insisted that Russia is 'very eager' to play a significant but 'peaceful role' in global affairs, though reports suggest Russia seeks to expand its influence. He said Mr. Putin believes that the world 'should not be dominated' by a single country, contradicting the U.S. stance. Lavrov writes that 'many Russians' are concerned about why the U.S. feels threatened by NATO's expansion to Russia's border and the planned U.S. missile defense system in Poland and the Czech Republic. The White House insists the planned missile defense system in Eastern Europe is a 'direct threat' to Russia, contrary to their previous statements.

It's located 100 miles south of Islamabad, Pakistan's capital, and attracts up to 250,000 visitors each year. The mine was discovered in 320 BC by Alexander the Great's troops, with salt trading commencing in the 16th century during the Mughal era. Dr. Warth, a mining engineer, developed the main ground-level tunnel in 1872 under British rule. The mine remains Pakistan's largest salt source, producing over 350,000 tons annually.

According to the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), East Atlantic and Mediterranean bluefin tuna populations have declined by approximately 61% over the last decade. article_content: Researchers at Cambridge University have found that people's musical preferences are associated with their life stages. The study analyzed data from over 250,000 people and identified five categories of musical taste: 'mellow', 'unpretentious', 'sophisticated', 'intense', and 'contemporary'. Teenagers tend to prefer 'intense' music, such as punk and metal. Young adults shift towards 'contemporary' and 'mellow' genres like R&B. As people enter middle age, they often favor 'sophisticated' and 'unpretentious' music, such as jazz, classical, country, and folk.

article_content: Forget a draughty horse box or a muddy field. You're more likely to find this little chap warming his flanks by the fire or nuzzling the crumbs under the kitchen table. At 22 inches tall, Acer is the perfect house pet size, and barely as big as his best friend, his owner's black labrador, Demon. As a result, he enjoys all the comforts of home. Acer, now aged three, was born with dwarfism, caused by a recessive gene that only affects a foal when it's carried by both parents. Standing tall: Little Acer stands next to a normal-sized horse in the field next to the Miniature Horse Farm. Most dwarfism foals are put down due to health problems, such as skeletal issues and shortened life expectancy, but his owner, Maureen O'Sullivan, who runs the Miniature Horse Farm in Corringham, Essex, couldn't bear to part with him. She said: 'We imported his dad from America and put him with our American mare, and they must both have been carrying the dwarf gene – he was the result.' 'Due to dwarves having various health issues, most breeders would have put him down, but little Acer was so full of life and otherwise healthy, it was never an option.' 'One day we were in the living room, and he just wandered in; we were really surprised. Thanks to his size, Maureen can simply take Acer for a walk on his lead in the nearby fields. The horse, believed to be Britain's smallest, can even fit into the family car for a run out. Acer sniffs at a treat with his best friend, Demon the black labrador in Maureen's kitchen. 'When he comes in, he loves to watch the television; he just stands there staring at it. He likes to walk around and sniff everything, so now we let him come and go as he wants.' Although he's more than welcome to wander around the house, Acer does have his own traditional stable at the farm. But it does cater to his size with the tiniest of stable doors, so he can see out onto the yard. Miss O'Sullivan said: 'We had the door specially made for him so he can put his head over and see all the other horses.' Acer gets close to Maureen as she takes him for a spin on the back of a golf buggy around the farm.
translated_content: Acer is a 3-year-old miniature horse with dwarfism. He is 22 inches tall and lives with his owner Maureen O'Sullivan at the Miniature Horse Farm in Corringham, Essex. Maureen said: 'Acer was born with dwarfism due to a recessive gene carried by both his parents.' Acer enjoys the comforts of home and loves to watch TV and explore the house.

article_content: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday refused to entertain a plea seeking a direction to the Centre to make guidelines for 'protection' of Hinduism in India. A bench headed by Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul said the apex court was not inclined to entertain such a petition. The court noted that if it entertained this plea, similar requests might be made for other religions. The petitioner, an Uttar Pradesh-based man, appeared in person to argue his case. The bench, also comprising Justices Sudhanshu Dhulia and Ahsanuddin Amanullah, observed that the petitioner cannot dictate the actions of others. 'You can propagate your views, but you can't compel others to follow,' the court said, dismissing the plea.
